problems.title: The five questions

options: dp[a] = the fewest coins summing to exactly a
dp[a] = the coins used so far
dp[a] = 1 + min over coins c ≤ a of dp[a − c]

problems.solution: State, transition by the last coin, and base dp[0] = 0. The answer is dp[amount], or −1 if it is still the sentinel.

problems.title: Robber
problems.solution: [2, 1, 1, 2]: take both ends = 4 (the alternating choice gives 3). [6, 1, 2, 7, 3]: 6 + 7 = 13.

problems.title: Greedy fails

parts.prompt: Greedy (largest first) uses how many coins?

problems.solution: Greedy takes 4, 1, 1 for 3 coins; DP finds 3 + 3 = 2 coins.

problems.title: Coin table

parts.prompt: Largest amount that is impossible (the Frobenius number, 3·7 − 3 − 7)?

problems.solution: 20 needs 4 coins. 11 is impossible: neither 11, 4 nor −3 is a multiple of 3. The largest impossible amount is 11.

problems.title: LIS
problems.solution: Length 4. tails evolves 3 → 1 → 1 8 → 1 2 → 1 2 5 → 1 2 5 9 → 1 2 4 9 → 1 2 4 6. tails isn't necessarily a real subsequence (here it happens to be).

problems.title: Top-down or bottom-up?
problems.statement: n = 10⁵, dp[i] depends on dp[i−1] and dp[i−2], in Python.
problems.solution: Top-down would recurse 10⁵ deep, past Python's limit. Bottom-up is O(1) memory.

problems.title: Decode ways
hints: dp[i] = dp[i−1] if s[i−1] ≠ '0', + dp[i−2] if s[i−2:i] is in 10..26.

problems.title: Dominance
problems.statement: Why does the O(n log n) LIS keep only the smallest tail for each length?

options: Any element that extends a subsequence with a larger tail also extends one with a smaller tail

hints: Compare two subsequences of the same length.
problems.solution: A smaller tail dominates: it is never worse for the future. Throwing dominated states away is a general DP speed-up.
